flashcards.q: B+Tree vs LSM-Tree: the one-sentence structural difference?
flashcards.a: B+Tree updates in place and stays sorted on disk at all times; LSM-Tree never updates in place, writing to an in-memory memtable then flushing immutable sorted SSTables, deferring reorganization to background compaction.

flashcards.q: B-Tree fanout formula and typical value?
flashcards.a: fanout ≈ page_size / (key_size + pointer_size). For a 16KB InnoDB page, 16-byte key, 8-byte pointer: fanout ≈ 680.

flashcards.q: B-Tree height for 100M rows at fanout ~680?
flashcards.a: log_680(100,000,000) ≈ 3 levels. With upper levels cached, warm lookup is ~1-2 real disk I/Os, not literal log N reads.

flashcards.q: Define write amplification, read amplification, space amplification.
flashcards.a: WA = physical bytes written / logical bytes written. RA = disk reads per logical read. SA = physical bytes on disk / logical live bytes.

flashcards.q: Typical amplification numbers: B-Tree vs LSM (leveled)?
flashcards.a: B-Tree: WA ~3-4x, RA ~1-2x, SA ~1.1-1.5x. LSM leveled: WA ~20-30x+, RA ~1-2x with tuned bloom filters (5-10x+ without), SA ~1.1-1.3x tuned (spikes ~2x mid-compaction).

Size-tiered: lower write amplification (~10-15x) but overlapping key ranges raise read amplification and space can spike ~2x. Leveled: higher write amplification (~20-30x+) but non-overlapping levels give lower read amplification and tighter space usage.

flashcards.q: What is Time-Window Compaction Strategy (TWCS) and when do you use it?
flashcards.a: Buckets SSTables by time window, compacts only within a window, and drops whole expired files instead of rewriting them. Right choice for time-series data with uniform TTL expiry.

flashcards.q: What does a bloom filter buy an LSM-Tree, with real numbers?
flashcards.a: Probabilistic 'definitely not present / maybe present' check per SSTable. RocksDB default ~10 bits/key gives ~1% false positive rate, letting reads skip disk I/O on ~99% of files that don't contain the key.

flashcards.q: RUM conjecture — what does it say?
flashcards.a: Read, Update, Memory (space) amplification cannot all be minimized simultaneously — optimizing any two makes the third worse. It's a proven tradeoff, not an engineering habit.

flashcards.q: What causes B-Tree write amplification mechanically?
flashcards.a: A single row update dirties an entire page (8-16KB), and the whole page gets flushed even though only a fraction logically changed; a page split doubles this by dirtying two pages.

flashcards.q: Which real systems use B+Tree vs LSM storage?
flashcards.a: B+Tree family: Postgres, MySQL/InnoDB, SQL Server. LSM family: Cassandra, RocksDB-backed stores (MyRocks, TiKV, CockroachDB's Pebble/RocksDB), ScyllaDB.

flashcards.q: Leading indicator that an LSM store's read latency is about to degrade?
flashcards.a: L0 file count or pending-compaction-bytes climbing — compaction has fallen behind ingest. Instrument and alert on this before it shows up in read p99.

flashcards.q: Workload fit rule of thumb for choosing storage engine family?
flashcards.a: OLTP / read-heavy / mixed workloads -> B+Tree (Postgres, InnoDB). Write-firehose / high-ingest / logs / time-series -> LSM (Cassandra, RocksDB). Large analytical scans -> neither; columnar storage.

flashcards.q: Why can L0 SSTables be more expensive to read from than lower levels?
flashcards.a: L0 files are flushed independently from separate memtable snapshots, so their key ranges can overlap; a point read may need to check every L0 file, unlike lower levels (leveled compaction) where each level has non-overlapping ranges.

flashcards.q: Default page sizes: Postgres vs InnoDB?
flashcards.a: Postgres: 8 KB pages. InnoDB: 16 KB pages by default.
